## Definition of a Regular Convex Polyhedron

Let $P$ be a convex $m$-dimensional polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^k$.

### Flags

A **flag** of $P$ is a maximal chain of mutually incident faces, containing exactly one face of each dimension $0, 1, \dots, m$. Formally, a flag is a tuple
$$\Phi = (F_0, F_1, \dots, F_m)$$
where:
- $F_i$ is an $i$-dimensional face of $P$ for each $i = 0, 1, \dots, m$,
- $F_0 \subsetneq F_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq F_m = P$,
- $F_0$ is a vertex, $F_1$ is an edge containing $F_0$, $F_2$ is a 2-face containing $F_1$, and so on, with $F_{m-1}$ a facet and $F_m = P$ itself.

Equivalently, a flag selects one vertex, one edge through that vertex, one 2-face through that edge, and so forth up to the entire polyhedron. The set of all flags of $P$ is denoted $\mathcal{F}(P)$.

### Rotational Symmetry Group

The **rotational symmetry group** $G(P)$ of $P$ is the group of all isometries of $\mathbb{R}^k$ that map $P$ onto itself:
$$G(P) = \{\, g : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k \mid g \text{ is an isometry and } g(P) = P \,\}.$$

When $k > m$, every symmetry of the $m$-dimensional polyhedron $P$ — including reflections within the $m$-dimensional affine subspace containing $P$ — can be realized as a rotation (orientation-preserving isometry) in the ambient $k$-dimensional space. This is because an $m$-dimensional reflection extends to a $k$-dimensional rotation by rotating in the 2-plane spanned by the reflection normal and an extra direction perpendicular to the $m$-flat. Thus, when $k > m$, $G(P)$ consists entirely of rotations of $\mathbb{R}^k$ and coincides with the full symmetry group of $P$.

### Regularity

The polyhedron $P$ is **regular** if and only if $G(P)$ acts **transitively** on the set of flags $\mathcal{F}(P)$:

$$\forall\, \Phi, \Phi' \in \mathcal{F}(P),\ \ \exists\, g \in G(P) \text{ such that } g(F_i) = F'_i \text{ for all } i = 0, 1, \dots, m.$$

In other words, for any two flags $\Phi = (F_0, \dots, F_m)$ and $\Phi' = (F'_0, \dots, F'_m)$, there is a symmetry $g \in G(P)$ that maps each face $F_i$ of the first flag to the corresponding face $F'_i$ of the second.

### Meaning of the Condition

Flag-transitivity is the strongest possible homogeneity condition on a polyhedron: it says that every local incidence configuration — one face of each dimension, all nested — is geometrically indistinguishable from every other. The polyhedron "looks the same" when viewed from any flag. This single condition implies the more familiar consequences of regularity:

- **Vertex-transitivity**: $G(P)$ acts transitively on vertices (project any flag to its $F_0$).
- **Face-transitivity in every dimension**: $G(P)$ acts transitively on $i$-faces for each $i$ (project any flag to its $F_i$).
- **Uniformity of vertex figures**: the vertex figure at every vertex is congruent (it is determined by the flag up to symmetry).
- **Recursive regularity**: every facet $F_{m-1}$ is itself a regular $(m-1)$-polyhedron, and every vertex figure is a regular $(m-1)$-polyhedron.

Conversely, for convex polytopes, these weaker conditions together imply flag-transitivity, so the definition is robust: regularity = flag-transitivity of the symmetry group.

## Definition of a Regular Convex Polyhedron

Let $P$ be a convex $m$-dimensional polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^k$.

### Flags

A **flag** of $P$ is a maximal chain of mutually incident faces, containing exactly one face of each dimension $0, 1, \dots, m$. Formally, a flag is a tuple
$$\Phi = (F_0, F_1, \dots, F_m)$$
where:
- $F_i$ is an $i$-dimensional face of $P$ for each $i = 0, 1, \dots, m$,
- $F_0 \subsetneq F_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq F_m = P$,
- $F_0$ is a vertex, $F_1$ is an edge containing $F_0$, $F_2$ is a 2-face containing $F_1$, and so on, with $F_{m-1}$ a facet and $F_m = P$ itself.

Equivalently, a flag selects one vertex, one edge through that vertex, one 2-face through that edge, and so forth up to the entire polyhedron. The set of all flags of $P$ is denoted $\mathcal{F}(P)$.

### Rotational Symmetry Group

The **rotational symmetry group** $G(P)$ of $P$ is the group of all isometries of $\mathbb{R}^k$ that map $P$ onto itself:
$$G(P) = \{\, g : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k \mid g \text{ is an isometry and } g(P) = P \,\}.$$

When $k > m$, every symmetry of the $m$-dimensional polyhedron $P$ — including reflections within the $m$-dimensional affine subspace containing $P$ — can be realized as a rotation (orientation-preserving isometry) in the ambient $k$-dimensional space. This is because an $m$-dimensional reflection extends to a $k$-dimensional rotation by rotating in the 2-plane spanned by the reflection normal and an extra direction perpendicular to the $m$-flat. Thus, when $k > m$, $G(P)$ consists entirely of rotations of $\mathbb{R}^k$ and coincides with the full symmetry group of $P$.

### Regularity

The polyhedron $P$ is **regular** if and only if $G(P)$ acts **transitively** on the set of flags $\mathcal{F}(P)$:

$$\forall\, \Phi, \Phi' \in \mathcal{F}(P),\ \ \exists\, g \in G(P) \text{ such that } g(F_i) = F'_i \text{ for all } i = 0, 1, \dots, m.$$

In other words, for any two flags $\Phi = (F_0, \dots, F_m)$ and $\Phi' = (F'_0, \dots, F'_m)$, there is a symmetry $g \in G(P)$ that maps each face $F_i$ of the first flag to the corresponding face $F'_i$ of the second.

### Meaning of the Condition

Flag-transitivity is the strongest possible homogeneity condition on a polyhedron: it says that every local incidence configuration — one face of each dimension, all nested — is geometrically indistinguishable from every other. The polyhedron "looks the same" when viewed from any flag. This single condition implies the more familiar consequences of regularity:

- **Vertex-transitivity**: $G(P)$ acts transitively on vertices (project any flag to its $F_0$).
- **Face-transitivity in every dimension**: $G(P)$ acts transitively on $i$-faces for each $i$ (project any flag to its $F_i$).
- **Uniformity of vertex figures**: the vertex figure at every vertex is congruent (it is determined by the flag up to symmetry).
- **Recursive regularity**: every facet $F_{m-1}$ is itself a regular $(m-1)$-polyhedron, and every vertex figure is a regular $(m-1)$-polyhedron.

Conversely, for convex polytopes, these weaker conditions together imply flag-transitivity, so the definition is robust: regularity = flag-transitivity of the symmetry group.
